claims.text: The macroeconomic aims of government are the economy-wide outcomes a government works towards: low inflation, low unemployment, steady growth in the output of the economy, a current account close to balance, and redistribution of income towards a fairer distribution.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Each aim is read off an indicator: the rate of inflation measures movement towards or away from low inflation, the unemployment rate measures the jobs aim, the annual rise in real output measures growth, the current account balance measures external balance, and the change in the gap between high and low household incomes measures progress towards a fairer distribution of income.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Low inflation tends to protect the buying power of wages and savings and lets firms plan ahead; low unemployment raises household incomes, keeps skills from fading and lifts tax revenue while cutting support payments; steady growth raises the output and average incomes the economy can sustain; a current account close to balance means a country is not persistently spending more abroad than it earns; a fairer distribution of income narrows the gap between rich and poor households, so more households can afford basics such as food, schooling and clinic visits.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The importance of each aim varies with the economy's circumstances: where unemployment is high the jobs aim tends to lead the ranking, and where prices are rising fast the inflation aim tends to lead.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A conflict between macroeconomic aims is a situation in which the conditions that serve one aim make another harder to achieve, so a government pushing towards one aim moves away from another at the same time.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A quick rise in spending across the economy tends to create jobs and raise output, but where capacity is tight the same pressure tends to push prices up, and part of the extra spending goes abroad on imports, which strains the inflation aim and the current account together.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Aims can move together instead of conflicting: growth built on rising productivity can raise output while adding little to price pressure, which serves the growth aim and the inflation aim at once.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A possible cause and a consequence are two ends of one relationship running in opposite directions: a quick rise in spending across the economy can be a cause of faster rises in prices, while faster rises in prices are the consequence of it; the test is to ask whether a named item sets the change in motion or follows from it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Governments choose growth because more output can raise jobs, incomes and tax revenue where gains are widely shared. They seek balance of payments stability because persistent current-account deficits require sustainable financing; borrowing can increase debt, while foreign investment or reserves can also finance a gap. Under a fixed exchange rate, reserves may fall if other inflows do not cover external payments. Redistribution can reduce poverty and widen access to schooling and healthcare.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Governments turn each aim into a measurable criterion: an inflation rate target such as 2% a year or a range such as 3% to 6%, a target unemployment rate, a target annual rise in real GDP, a current account deficit kept below a stated share of GDP, and a rise in the income share of the poorest households; a target shows whether policy is working, makes the government accountable, and, where people believe it, tends to steady expectations of price rises.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Three conflicts between aims arise from more spending across the economy: falling unemployment tends to push up wages and, where output cannot keep up, prices; growth raises incomes and spending on imports, widening the current account deficit where exports do not rise as fast; and fuller employment raises spending on imports and, where wages rise faster than in trading partners, makes exports dearer; where there is spare capacity, or extra output is sold abroad, the conflicts tend to be weaker.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
